## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) {auto-animate="true"} ### First Principal Direction $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}$ :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [**PCA**]{.light-blue} is a process of representing $X$ in a new coordinate system such that: - Each column has maximum variation along its direction. - All columns are **perpendicular/independent**. :::{.fragment .br20} :::{.callout-tip icon="false"} #### Objective of PCA - Without loss of generality, assume $X$ is centered: $\overline{X}_j=0,\forall j=1,\dots,d$. - [**Objective:**]{.blue} Finding $\color{blue}{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ such that $$\tilde{X}=X\color{blue}{U}\text{ s.t: }\begin{cases}\|\tilde{X}_j\|^2\text{ is maximized}\\\tilde{X}_j\perp\tilde{X}_k,\forall j\neq k.\end{cases}$$ :::{.up2} ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%" .fragment} - The objective of PCA can be reduced to finding each column of $\color{blue}{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$. :::{.callout-note icon="false" .br20} #### First Principal Direction $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}$ - We define the [**1st principal direction**]{.blue} $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$: $$\begin{align*}\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}&=\arg\max_{\vec{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|\vec{w}\|=1}\|X\vec{w}\|^2\\ &=\arg\max_{\vec{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|\vec{w}\|=1}\vec{w}^TX^TX\vec{w}.\end{align*}$$ :::{.up2} ::: ::: :::{.fragment} - This problem can be solved using [**Lagragian Method**]{.blue} 👇 :::{.hline style="font-size: 80%" .secbr} [📚 Hertzman et al. (2015)](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~mbrubake/teaching/C11/Handouts/LagrangeMultipliers.pdf){target="_blank"}
[📚 Appendix E. of Bishop et al. (2006)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2006/01/Bishop-Pattern-Recognition-and-Machine-Learning-2006.pdf){target="_blank"}. ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) {auto-animate="true"} ### Lagragian Method for $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}$ :::{style="font-size: 75%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} :::{.fragment} - Problem: Find $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ such that :::{.callout-note icon="false" appearance="minimal" .br20} $$\begin{align*}\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}&=\arg\max_{\vec{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|\vec{w}\|=1}\vec{w}^TX^TX\vec{w}.\end{align*}$$ ::: ::: :::{.fragment} - **Lagragian** at $\color{red}{\vec{w}}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\color{red}{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}$, [$$\begin{align*} {\cal L}(\color{red}{\vec{w}},\color{red}{\lambda})&=f(\color{red}{\vec{w}})+\color{red}{\lambda} g(\color{red}{\vec{w}})\\ &=\color{red}{\vec{w}}^TX^TX\color{red}{\vec{w}}+\color{red}{\lambda}(1-\|\color{red}{\vec{w}}\|^2)\\ &=\color{red}{\vec{w}}^TX^TX\color{red}{\vec{w}}+\color{red}{\lambda}(1-\color{red}{\vec{w}}^T\color{red}{\vec{w}}).\end{align*}$$]{.up3} ::: :::{.fragment .up2} - The solution may be obtained by setting the derivatives (gradients) of $\cal L$ to 0 i.e., $\nabla {\cal L}=0$. ::: ::: :::{.column width="45%"} :::{.fragment} :::{.callout-note icon="false" appearance="minimal" .br10} - Verify that the solution $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\color{blue}{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}$ of the system [$$\begin{cases}\frac{\partial {\cal L}(\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1},\color{blue}{\lambda})}{\partial \color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}}=0\\ \frac{\partial {\cal L}(\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1},\color{blue}{\lambda})}{\partial \color{blue}{\lambda}}=0\end{cases},$$]{.up2} satisfies $X^TX\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}=\color{blue}{\lambda\vec{u}_1}.$ - This implies that the [**1st principal direction**]{.blue} $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}$ is the [**eigenvector**]{.light-blue} of $X^TX$ for the [**eigenvalue**]{.light-blue} $\color{blue}{\lambda}$. ::: ```{python} fig1.update_layout(height=250, width=500) fig1.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) {auto-animate="true"} ### $k$-th principal direction $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_k}, k\geq 2$ :::{style="font-size: 90%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.callout-note icon="false" .br20 style="font-size: 95%"} #### $k$-th Principal direction $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_k}$ - For any $k\in\{2,\dots,d\}$, let $$\color{red}{\widehat{X}_k}=X-\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}X\color{blue}{\vec{u}_j\color{blue}{\vec{u}_j^T}},$$ then the $k$-th [**Principal direction**]{.blue} $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_k}$ is the unit vector, **orthogonal** to $\{\color{blue}{\vec{u}_j}:1\leq j\leq k-1\}$, and the variation of projected data on its direction is maximized: $$\begin{align*}\color{blue}{\vec{u}_k}&=\arg\max_{\vec{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|\vec{w}\|=1}\vec{w}^T\color{red}{\widehat{X}_k^T\widehat{X}_k}\vec{w}.\end{align*}$$ :::{.up2} ::: ::: :::{.br10 style="font-size: 80%"} - [**Proof:**]{.blue} Using Lagragian multiplier just like the case of $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}$. ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%" style="font-size: 80%" .fragment} :::{.callout-tip icon="false" style="font-size: 120%" .incremental} #### Solution to PCA problem - Solution to our original problem is $$\color{blue}{U}=[\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}| \color{blue}{\vec{u}_2| \dots | \color{blue}{\vec{u}_d}}]\in\mathbb{R}^d.$$ where $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_j}$ is the $j$-th **eigenvector** of $X^TX$ corresponding to **eigenvalue** $\color{blue}{\lambda_j}>0$. - The rotated data is defined by: $$\color{blue}{\tilde{X}}=X\color{blue}{U}.$$ - The variation along each direction $$\sum_{j=1}^d\|X_j\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\|\color{blue}{\tilde{X}_j}\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\color{blue}{\lambda_j^2}$$ :::{.sbr} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) {auto-animate="true"} ### Implementing PCA :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.callout-tip icon="false" style="font-size: 120%"} #### Unnormalized PCA - Given data: $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ - Centering $X_c=\underbrace{X}_{n\times d} -\underbrace{\mathbb{1}_n}_{n\times n}\underbrace{X}_{n\times d}/n.$ - Perform [**Eigenvalue Decomposition**](https://tobydriscoll.net/fnc-julia/matrixanaly/evd.html){target='_blank'} on covariance matrix $V=X_c^TX_c$: $$V=\color{blue}{U}\Sigma \color{blue}{U}^T,$$ - $\color{blue}{U}$: matrix of eigenvectors - $\Sigma=\text{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d)$: diagonal matrix of eigenvalues $\lambda_1\geq \dots\geq \lambda_d\geq 0$. ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.callout-tip icon="false" style="font-size: 120%" .fragment} #### Normalized PCA - Given data: $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ - Standardizing: compute std matrix $D=\text{diag}(\widehat{\sigma}_1,\dots,\widehat{\sigma}_d)$ and standardized data $Z=(\underbrace{X}_{n\times d} -\underbrace{\mathbb{1}_n}_{n\times n}\underbrace{X}_{n\times d}/n)D^{-1}.$ - Perform [**Eigenvalue Decomposition**](https://tobydriscoll.net/fnc-julia/matrixanaly/evd.html){target='_blank'} on correlation matrix $C=Z^TZ/(n-1)$: $$C=\color{blue}{U}\Sigma \color{blue}{U}^T.$$ - Rotated data: $\color{blue}{\tilde{X}}=X\color{blue}{U}.$ [👉 [Demo](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1M4JFHP5Y43uw3dQlyYbiD68wAtybS0Kw?usp=sharing){target="_blank"}] :::{.sbr} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) {auto-animate="true"} ### Dimensional reduction/Reconstruction :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} #### Dimensional Reduction - **Reduction** to $k$ dimensions ($k\dots>\lambda_d$. - Our goal is to explore dimensional reduction and reconstruction power of `PCA`, however, it can be used in Data Analysis, EDA, Data Summary... - **Remark:** Many highly correlated columns indicates effective dimensional reduction (the first two PCs can capture significant variation). ::: # $t$-Stochastic Neighbor Embedding ($t$-SNE) {background-color="#15797A"} ## $t$-SNE ### Setting :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%" .incremental} - Suppose $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ with large $d$. :::{.callout-tip icon="false" style="font-size: 120%" .br10 .fragment} #### Objective **$t$-SNE** aims at finding **lower dimensional** (LD) representation of $X$ (2 or 3) so that the distribution among LD data is similar to the original data. ::: - [Hinton and Roweis (2002)](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~fritz/absps/sne.pdf){target="_blank"} proposed Stochastic Embedding Neighbor (SNE) and $t$-SNE is its improved version [see [Laurens, $t$-SNE Page](https://lvdmaaten.github.io/tsne/){target="_blank"}]. ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.r-stack} :::{.fragment .br10} ```{python} #| eval: true from keras import datasets import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = datasets.mnist.load_data() X = x_train.reshape(60000, -1) fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(6, 3.5)) IDs = np.random.randint(0,60000, size=12) for i,j in enumerate(IDs): axes[i//4, i%4].imshow(x_train[j,:,:], cmap="viridis") axes[i//4, i%4].axis('off') axes[i//4, i%4].set_title(f"Label: {y_train[j]}") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: :::{.br20} :::{.fragment} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| eval: true from sklearn.manifold import TSNE # Prepare the t-SNE model tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, random_state=42) # Fit and transform the data X_tsne = tsne.fit_transform(X[:1000,:]) # Use a subset for faster computation df_tsne = pd.DataFrame(X_tsne, columns=['Component 1', 'Component 2']) df_tsne['label'] = y_train[:1000] fig_tsne = px.scatter(df_tsne, x="Component 1", y="Component 2", color="label") fig_tsne.update_layout(height=420, width=550, title="t-SNE visualization on MNIST") fig_tsne.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## $t$-SNE ### [Original]{.light-blue} and [embedding]{.light-red} distribution in $t$-SNE :::{.colums} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 60%" .incremental} 1. Pairwise similarities in the original space: - [**Conditional probabilities (Gaussian):**]{.blue} for any $\color{purple}{\text{x}_i}\in\mathbb{R}^d$, the chance that $\text{x}_j$ is its neighbor: [$$p_{j|\color{purple}{i}}=\frac{e^{-\|\text{x}_j-\color{purple}{\text{x}_i}\|^2/(2\sigma_{\color{purple}{i}}^2)}}{\sum_{k\neq \color{purple}{i}}^n e^{-\|\text{x}_k-\color{purple}{\text{x}_i}\|^2/(2\sigma_{\color{purple}{i}}^2)}}$$]{.up1 style="font-size: 120%"} [with $\sigma_{\color{purple}{i}}>0$ defining the surrounding area of $\color{purple}{\text{x}_i}$.]{style="font-size: 95%"} - [**Symmetric probabilities:**]{.blue} $\displaystyle \color{blue}{p_{i,j}}=\frac{p_{j|\color{purple}{i}}+p_{i|\color{purple}{j}}}{2n}.$ [$$\color{blue}{P} = \begin{bmatrix}\color{blue}{p_{1,1}} & \color{blue}{p_{1,2}} & \color{blue}{...} & \color{blue}{p_{1,n}}\\ \color{blue}{p_{2,1}} & \color{blue}{p_{2,2}} & \color{blue}{...} & \color{blue}{p_{2,n}}\\ \color{blue}{\vdots} & \color{blue}{\vdots} & \color{blue}{\ddots} & \color{blue}{\vdots}\\ \color{blue}{p_{n,1}} & \color{blue}{p_{n,2}} & \color{blue}{...} & \color{blue}{p_{n,n}}\end{bmatrix}$$]{.up1 style="font-size: 120%"} ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 57%" .incremental} 2. [**Objective of $t$-SNE:**]{.darkgreen} find low-dimensional data points $\color{red}{\text{z}_1},\dots, \color{red}{\text{z}_n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ ($d' ## $t$-SNE ### Summary :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} - [**$t$-SNE**]{.blue} is a non-linear dimentional reduction technique aiming at searching for neighbors of points in a lower-dimensional space (2 or 3) especially for visualization. - High-dimensional data $X$ is converted to pairwise similarity probability $\color{blue}{P=(p_{i,j})}$ according to how close they are. - The pairwise similarity probability $\color{red}{Q=(q_{i,j})}$ of low-dimensional data points is defined based on $t$-distribution of degree 1 or Cauchy distribution. - The proximity between $\color{blue}{P}$ and $\color{red}{Q}$ is measured using **KL divergence**. - The LD data $z_i$ are estimated by minimizing **KL divergence** using **Gradient Descent with Momontum**. - Understand more about $t$-SNE: [**Laurens van der Maaten's t-SNE Page**](https://lvdmaaten.github.io/tsne/){target="_blank"} and [How to Use t-SNE Effectively, Distill, Google Brain Team](https://distill.pub/2016/misread-tsne/){target="_blank"}. ::: # Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (JL) {background-color="#15797A"} ## Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (JL) ### Setting :::{.incremental} - Given data points: $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ - [**JL lemma:**]{.blue} result allows us to project data $\color{blue}{\text{x}_i},\color{blue}{\text{x}_j}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ onto a smaller subspace $\color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_i}, \color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ with $d'0$: $$\mathbb{P}_{\color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_i},\color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_j}}\left(\left|\frac{\|\color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_i}-\color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_j}\|_{d'}^2}{\|\color{blue}{\text{x}_i}-\color{blue}{\text{x}_j}\|_d^2}-1\right|>\varepsilon\right)\text{ is small}.$$ ::: ## Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (JL) ### [Lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson%E2%80%93Lindenstrauss_lemma) :::{.incremental} :::{.callout-tip icon="false" style='font-size: 110%'} #### Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (Gaussian matrix projection) Let $X=\{\color{blue}{\text{x}_1,\dots,\text{x}_n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be $n$ points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$, and let ${\cal G}=(G_{i,j})$ with $G_{k,j}\overset{iid}{\sim}{\cal N}(0,1/\color{red}{d'})$ for $k=1,\dots,d$ and $j=1,\dots,\color{red}{d'}$ with $\color{red}{d'} \varepsilon\right)< 2ne^{-\color{red}{d'}(\varepsilon^2/2-\varepsilon^3/3)}.$$ :::{.sbr} ::: ::: - Proof: see for example: [Kevin (2016)](https://www.math.toronto.edu/undergrad/projects-undergrad/Project03.pdf){target='_blank'} or [Has (2022)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.02606){target="_blank"}. ::: ## Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (JL) ### When should we consider JL? :::{.incremental style="font-size: 80%"} - [**JL lemma**]{.light-blue} focuses on [**preserving pair of Euclidean distances**]{.light-blue} between data points when projecting. - It's suitable for problem involving measuring Euclidean distances between high-dimensional data points: $k$-NN, KMeans clustering, Kernel smoothing methods... [👉 [Demo](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1M4JFHP5Y43uw3dQlyYbiD68wAtybS0Kw?usp=sharing){target="_blank"}] :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%" .fragment} ```{python} #| fig-align: center from sklearn.metrics import pairwise_distances np.random.seed(12) X1 = np.random.normal(size=(5,3)) X1_proj = X1 @ np.random.normal(0,1/np.sqrt(2), size=(3,2)) fig4 = go.Figure( go.Scatter3d(x=X1[:,0], y=X1[:,1], z=X1[:,2], mode='markers', showlegend = False, marker=dict(size=5, color=[i for i in range(5)]), name="3D data") ) fig4.add_trace( go.Scatter3d(x=X1_proj[:,0], y=X1_proj[:,1], z=np.zeros(5)-2.5, mode='markers', showlegend = False, marker=dict(size=5, symbol='diamond', color=[i for i in range(5)]), name="2D data") ) fig4.update_layout(height=300, width=500, title="JL Lemma from 3D to 2D") fig4.show() ``` ::: :::{.column width="50%" .fragment} ```{python} #| fig-align: center np.random.seed(12) dist = np.zeros(shape=(5000,4)) X1 = np.random.normal(size=(5,3)) dis0 = pairwise_distances(X1) for i in range(5000): X1_proj = X1 @ np.random.normal(0,1/np.sqrt(2), size=(3,2)) dis = pairwise_distances(X1_proj) dist[i,:] = dis[0,1:]/dis0[0,1:] D = [dist[:,i] for i in range(4)] group_labels = ['dist' + str(i) for i in range(4)] import plotly.figure_factory as ff fig5 = ff.create_distplot(D, group_labels, bin_size=.1) fig5.update_layout(height=300, width=500, title="Distribution of distance ratio") fig5.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: # AutoEncoders {background-color="#15797A"} ## AutoEncoders {auto-animate="true"} ### Introduction :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} [![](./img/Autoencoders1.png)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.05991){target='_blank'} [![](./img/Autoencoders2.png)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.03898){target='_blank'} ::: :::{.column width="50%" .incremental} - [**AutoEncoders:**]{.blue} are a type of DNN used for learning efficient codings of input data. - It's an unsupervised learning method that works by compressing data into a lower-dimensional representation (encoding) and then reconstructing it back to its original form (decoding). :::{.fragment} ![](./img/encoded_6.png){fig-align="center"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## AutoEncoders {auto-animate="true"} ### Main components / Loss :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%" .incremental} ![](./img/encoded_6.png){fig-align="center"} - Data: $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$. - [**Encoder:**]{.blue} $E:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ encodes original data into lower-dimensional representation called **Latent Representation**. - [**Decoder:**]{.blue} $D:\mathbb{R}^{d'}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ reconstructs back the original data from their **Latent Representation**. ::: :::{.column width="50%" .incremental .fragment} ### Loss - Training optimal $\color{blue}{E^*}$ and $\color{blue}{D^*}$ networks can be simply formulated as: $$(\color{blue}{E^*},\color{blue}{D^*})=\arg\min_{E,D} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\text{x}_i,D[E(\text{x}_i)]).$$ - This is equivalent to training two neural networks at once. - **AE** is in fact a generalization of PCA, while PCA finds the optimal linear subs-space (hyperplane) for the projected data, **AE** is able to learn non-linear **manifold embedding** [see [Elad Plaut (2018)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.10253){target="_blank"}]. ::: ::: ::: ## AutoEncoders {auto-animate="true"} ### Other types :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - [**Sparse Autoencoders:**]{.blue} $\color{blue}{E^*}$ and $\color{blue}{D^*}$ networks are trained with penalization. - $L_1$ regularization for regression: $$(\color{blue}{E^*},\color{blue}{D^*})=\arg\min_{E,D} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\text{x}_i,D[E(\text{x}_i)])+\lambda\sum|\color{blue}{W}_{E,D}|.$$ - KL divergence for classification: $$(\color{blue}{E^*},\color{blue}{D^*})=\arg\min_{E,D} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\text{x}_i,D[E(\text{x}_i)])+\lambda\sum_{j}\color{blue}{\text{KL}}(p\|\hat{p}_j).$$ ::: ## AutoEncoders {auto-animate="true"} ### Other types :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - [**Denoising Autoencoders:**]{.blue} $\color{blue}{E^*}$ and $\color{blue}{D^*}$ networks are trained just like before, and the noisy input $\tilde{\text{x}}_i$ is obtained by, for example, $\tilde{\text{x}}_i\sim {\cal N}(\text{x}_i,\sigma^2I_d).$ ![](./img/denosing_ae.png){width=450 fig-align="center"} - [**Variational Autoencoders (VAE)**]{.blue}: see for example, [Diederik P. Kingma and Max Welling (2019)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.02691){target="_blank"}. [👉 [Demo](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1M4JFHP5Y43uw3dQlyYbiD68wAtybS0Kw?usp=sharing){target="_blank"}] ::: :::{.center} ## 🥳 It's party time 🥂 {background-image="./img/end_page.jpg" background-opacity="0.3"}

## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) {auto-animate="true"} ### First Principal Direction $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}$ :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [**PCA**]{.light-blue} is a process of representing $X$ in a new coordinate system such that: - Each column has maximum variation along its direction. - All columns are **perpendicular/independent**. :::{.fragment .br20} :::{.callout-tip icon="false"} #### Objective of PCA - Without loss of generality, assume $X$ is centered: $\overline{X}_j=0,\forall j=1,\dots,d$. - [**Objective:**]{.blue} Finding $\color{blue}{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ such that $$\tilde{X}=X\color{blue}{U}\text{ s.t: }\begin{cases}\|\tilde{X}_j\|^2\text{ is maximized}\\\tilde{X}_j\perp\tilde{X}_k,\forall j\neq k.\end{cases}$$ :::{.up2} ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%" .fragment} - The objective of PCA can be reduced to finding each column of $\color{blue}{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$. :::{.callout-note icon="false" .br20} #### First Principal Direction $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}$ - We define the [**1st principal direction**]{.blue} $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$: $$\begin{align*}\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}&=\arg\max_{\vec{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|\vec{w}\|=1}\|X\vec{w}\|^2\\ &=\arg\max_{\vec{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|\vec{w}\|=1}\vec{w}^TX^TX\vec{w}.\end{align*}$$ :::{.up2} ::: ::: :::{.fragment} - This problem can be solved using [**Lagragian Method**]{.blue} 👇 :::{.hline style="font-size: 80%" .secbr} [📚 Hertzman et al. (2015)](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~mbrubake/teaching/C11/Handouts/LagrangeMultipliers.pdf){target="_blank"}
[📚 Appendix E. of Bishop et al. (2006)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2006/01/Bishop-Pattern-Recognition-and-Machine-Learning-2006.pdf){target="_blank"}. ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) {auto-animate="true"} ### Lagragian Method for $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}$ :::{style="font-size: 75%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} :::{.fragment} - Problem: Find $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ such that :::{.callout-note icon="false" appearance="minimal" .br20} $$\begin{align*}\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}&=\arg\max_{\vec{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|\vec{w}\|=1}\vec{w}^TX^TX\vec{w}.\end{align*}$$ ::: ::: :::{.fragment} - **Lagragian** at $\color{red}{\vec{w}}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\color{red}{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}$, [$$\begin{align*} {\cal L}(\color{red}{\vec{w}},\color{red}{\lambda})&=f(\color{red}{\vec{w}})+\color{red}{\lambda} g(\color{red}{\vec{w}})\\ &=\color{red}{\vec{w}}^TX^TX\color{red}{\vec{w}}+\color{red}{\lambda}(1-\|\color{red}{\vec{w}}\|^2)\\ &=\color{red}{\vec{w}}^TX^TX\color{red}{\vec{w}}+\color{red}{\lambda}(1-\color{red}{\vec{w}}^T\color{red}{\vec{w}}).\end{align*}$$]{.up3} ::: :::{.fragment .up2} - The solution may be obtained by setting the derivatives (gradients) of $\cal L$ to 0 i.e., $\nabla {\cal L}=0$. ::: ::: :::{.column width="45%"} :::{.fragment} :::{.callout-note icon="false" appearance="minimal" .br10} - Verify that the solution $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\color{blue}{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}$ of the system [$$\begin{cases}\frac{\partial {\cal L}(\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1},\color{blue}{\lambda})}{\partial \color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}}=0\\ \frac{\partial {\cal L}(\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1},\color{blue}{\lambda})}{\partial \color{blue}{\lambda}}=0\end{cases},$$]{.up2} satisfies $X^TX\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}=\color{blue}{\lambda\vec{u}_1}.$ - This implies that the [**1st principal direction**]{.blue} $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}$ is the [**eigenvector**]{.light-blue} of $X^TX$ for the [**eigenvalue**]{.light-blue} $\color{blue}{\lambda}$. ::: ```{python} fig1.update_layout(height=250, width=500) fig1.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) {auto-animate="true"} ### $k$-th principal direction $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_k}, k\geq 2$ :::{style="font-size: 90%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.callout-note icon="false" .br20 style="font-size: 95%"} #### $k$-th Principal direction $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_k}$ - For any $k\in\{2,\dots,d\}$, let $$\color{red}{\widehat{X}_k}=X-\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}X\color{blue}{\vec{u}_j\color{blue}{\vec{u}_j^T}},$$ then the $k$-th [**Principal direction**]{.blue} $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_k}$ is the unit vector, **orthogonal** to $\{\color{blue}{\vec{u}_j}:1\leq j\leq k-1\}$, and the variation of projected data on its direction is maximized: $$\begin{align*}\color{blue}{\vec{u}_k}&=\arg\max_{\vec{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|\vec{w}\|=1}\vec{w}^T\color{red}{\widehat{X}_k^T\widehat{X}_k}\vec{w}.\end{align*}$$ :::{.up2} ::: ::: :::{.br10 style="font-size: 80%"} - [**Proof:**]{.blue} Using Lagragian multiplier just like the case of $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}$. ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%" style="font-size: 80%" .fragment} :::{.callout-tip icon="false" style="font-size: 120%" .incremental} #### Solution to PCA problem - Solution to our original problem is $$\color{blue}{U}=[\color{blue}{\vec{u}_1}| \color{blue}{\vec{u}_2| \dots | \color{blue}{\vec{u}_d}}]\in\mathbb{R}^d.$$ where $\color{blue}{\vec{u}_j}$ is the $j$-th **eigenvector** of $X^TX$ corresponding to **eigenvalue** $\color{blue}{\lambda_j}>0$. - The rotated data is defined by: $$\color{blue}{\tilde{X}}=X\color{blue}{U}.$$ - The variation along each direction $$\sum_{j=1}^d\|X_j\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\|\color{blue}{\tilde{X}_j}\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\color{blue}{\lambda_j^2}$$ :::{.sbr} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) {auto-animate="true"} ### Implementing PCA :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.callout-tip icon="false" style="font-size: 120%"} #### Unnormalized PCA - Given data: $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ - Centering $X_c=\underbrace{X}_{n\times d} -\underbrace{\mathbb{1}_n}_{n\times n}\underbrace{X}_{n\times d}/n.$ - Perform [**Eigenvalue Decomposition**](https://tobydriscoll.net/fnc-julia/matrixanaly/evd.html){target='_blank'} on covariance matrix $V=X_c^TX_c$: $$V=\color{blue}{U}\Sigma \color{blue}{U}^T,$$ - $\color{blue}{U}$: matrix of eigenvectors - $\Sigma=\text{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d)$: diagonal matrix of eigenvalues $\lambda_1\geq \dots\geq \lambda_d\geq 0$. ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.callout-tip icon="false" style="font-size: 120%" .fragment} #### Normalized PCA - Given data: $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ - Standardizing: compute std matrix $D=\text{diag}(\widehat{\sigma}_1,\dots,\widehat{\sigma}_d)$ and standardized data $Z=(\underbrace{X}_{n\times d} -\underbrace{\mathbb{1}_n}_{n\times n}\underbrace{X}_{n\times d}/n)D^{-1}.$ - Perform [**Eigenvalue Decomposition**](https://tobydriscoll.net/fnc-julia/matrixanaly/evd.html){target='_blank'} on correlation matrix $C=Z^TZ/(n-1)$: $$C=\color{blue}{U}\Sigma \color{blue}{U}^T.$$ - Rotated data: $\color{blue}{\tilde{X}}=X\color{blue}{U}.$ [👉 [Demo](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1M4JFHP5Y43uw3dQlyYbiD68wAtybS0Kw?usp=sharing){target="_blank"}] :::{.sbr} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) {auto-animate="true"} ### Dimensional reduction/Reconstruction :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} #### Dimensional Reduction - **Reduction** to $k$ dimensions ($k\dots>\lambda_d$. - Our goal is to explore dimensional reduction and reconstruction power of `PCA`, however, it can be used in Data Analysis, EDA, Data Summary... - **Remark:** Many highly correlated columns indicates effective dimensional reduction (the first two PCs can capture significant variation). ::: # $t$-Stochastic Neighbor Embedding ($t$-SNE) {background-color="#15797A"} ## $t$-SNE ### Setting :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%" .incremental} - Suppose $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ with large $d$. :::{.callout-tip icon="false" style="font-size: 120%" .br10 .fragment} #### Objective **$t$-SNE** aims at finding **lower dimensional** (LD) representation of $X$ (2 or 3) so that the distribution among LD data is similar to the original data. ::: - [Hinton and Roweis (2002)](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~fritz/absps/sne.pdf){target="_blank"} proposed Stochastic Embedding Neighbor (SNE) and $t$-SNE is its improved version [see [Laurens, $t$-SNE Page](https://lvdmaaten.github.io/tsne/){target="_blank"}]. ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.r-stack} :::{.fragment .br10} ```{python} #| eval: true from keras import datasets import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = datasets.mnist.load_data() X = x_train.reshape(60000, -1) fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(6, 3.5)) IDs = np.random.randint(0,60000, size=12) for i,j in enumerate(IDs): axes[i//4, i%4].imshow(x_train[j,:,:], cmap="viridis") axes[i//4, i%4].axis('off') axes[i//4, i%4].set_title(f"Label: {y_train[j]}") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: :::{.br20} :::{.fragment} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| eval: true from sklearn.manifold import TSNE # Prepare the t-SNE model tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, random_state=42) # Fit and transform the data X_tsne = tsne.fit_transform(X[:1000,:]) # Use a subset for faster computation df_tsne = pd.DataFrame(X_tsne, columns=['Component 1', 'Component 2']) df_tsne['label'] = y_train[:1000] fig_tsne = px.scatter(df_tsne, x="Component 1", y="Component 2", color="label") fig_tsne.update_layout(height=420, width=550, title="t-SNE visualization on MNIST") fig_tsne.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## $t$-SNE ### [Original]{.light-blue} and [embedding]{.light-red} distribution in $t$-SNE :::{.colums} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 60%" .incremental} 1. Pairwise similarities in the original space: - [**Conditional probabilities (Gaussian):**]{.blue} for any $\color{purple}{\text{x}_i}\in\mathbb{R}^d$, the chance that $\text{x}_j$ is its neighbor: [$$p_{j|\color{purple}{i}}=\frac{e^{-\|\text{x}_j-\color{purple}{\text{x}_i}\|^2/(2\sigma_{\color{purple}{i}}^2)}}{\sum_{k\neq \color{purple}{i}}^n e^{-\|\text{x}_k-\color{purple}{\text{x}_i}\|^2/(2\sigma_{\color{purple}{i}}^2)}}$$]{.up1 style="font-size: 120%"} [with $\sigma_{\color{purple}{i}}>0$ defining the surrounding area of $\color{purple}{\text{x}_i}$.]{style="font-size: 95%"} - [**Symmetric probabilities:**]{.blue} $\displaystyle \color{blue}{p_{i,j}}=\frac{p_{j|\color{purple}{i}}+p_{i|\color{purple}{j}}}{2n}.$ [$$\color{blue}{P} = \begin{bmatrix}\color{blue}{p_{1,1}} & \color{blue}{p_{1,2}} & \color{blue}{...} & \color{blue}{p_{1,n}}\\ \color{blue}{p_{2,1}} & \color{blue}{p_{2,2}} & \color{blue}{...} & \color{blue}{p_{2,n}}\\ \color{blue}{\vdots} & \color{blue}{\vdots} & \color{blue}{\ddots} & \color{blue}{\vdots}\\ \color{blue}{p_{n,1}} & \color{blue}{p_{n,2}} & \color{blue}{...} & \color{blue}{p_{n,n}}\end{bmatrix}$$]{.up1 style="font-size: 120%"} ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 57%" .incremental} 2. [**Objective of $t$-SNE:**]{.darkgreen} find low-dimensional data points $\color{red}{\text{z}_1},\dots, \color{red}{\text{z}_n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ ($d' ## $t$-SNE ### Summary :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} - [**$t$-SNE**]{.blue} is a non-linear dimentional reduction technique aiming at searching for neighbors of points in a lower-dimensional space (2 or 3) especially for visualization. - High-dimensional data $X$ is converted to pairwise similarity probability $\color{blue}{P=(p_{i,j})}$ according to how close they are. - The pairwise similarity probability $\color{red}{Q=(q_{i,j})}$ of low-dimensional data points is defined based on $t$-distribution of degree 1 or Cauchy distribution. - The proximity between $\color{blue}{P}$ and $\color{red}{Q}$ is measured using **KL divergence**. - The LD data $z_i$ are estimated by minimizing **KL divergence** using **Gradient Descent with Momontum**. - Understand more about $t$-SNE: [**Laurens van der Maaten's t-SNE Page**](https://lvdmaaten.github.io/tsne/){target="_blank"} and [How to Use t-SNE Effectively, Distill, Google Brain Team](https://distill.pub/2016/misread-tsne/){target="_blank"}. ::: # Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (JL) {background-color="#15797A"} ## Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (JL) ### Setting :::{.incremental} - Given data points: $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ - [**JL lemma:**]{.blue} result allows us to project data $\color{blue}{\text{x}_i},\color{blue}{\text{x}_j}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ onto a smaller subspace $\color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_i}, \color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ with $d'0$: $$\mathbb{P}_{\color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_i},\color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_j}}\left(\left|\frac{\|\color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_i}-\color{red}{\widehat{\text{x}}_j}\|_{d'}^2}{\|\color{blue}{\text{x}_i}-\color{blue}{\text{x}_j}\|_d^2}-1\right|>\varepsilon\right)\text{ is small}.$$ ::: ## Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (JL) ### [Lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson%E2%80%93Lindenstrauss_lemma) :::{.incremental} :::{.callout-tip icon="false" style='font-size: 110%'} #### Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (Gaussian matrix projection) Let $X=\{\color{blue}{\text{x}_1,\dots,\text{x}_n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be $n$ points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$, and let ${\cal G}=(G_{i,j})$ with $G_{k,j}\overset{iid}{\sim}{\cal N}(0,1/\color{red}{d'})$ for $k=1,\dots,d$ and $j=1,\dots,\color{red}{d'}$ with $\color{red}{d'} \varepsilon\right)< 2ne^{-\color{red}{d'}(\varepsilon^2/2-\varepsilon^3/3)}.$$ :::{.sbr} ::: ::: - Proof: see for example: [Kevin (2016)](https://www.math.toronto.edu/undergrad/projects-undergrad/Project03.pdf){target='_blank'} or [Has (2022)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.02606){target="_blank"}. ::: ## Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (JL) ### When should we consider JL? :::{.incremental style="font-size: 80%"} - [**JL lemma**]{.light-blue} focuses on [**preserving pair of Euclidean distances**]{.light-blue} between data points when projecting. - It's suitable for problem involving measuring Euclidean distances between high-dimensional data points: $k$-NN, KMeans clustering, Kernel smoothing methods... [👉 [Demo](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1M4JFHP5Y43uw3dQlyYbiD68wAtybS0Kw?usp=sharing){target="_blank"}] :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%" .fragment} ```{python} #| fig-align: center from sklearn.metrics import pairwise_distances np.random.seed(12) X1 = np.random.normal(size=(5,3)) X1_proj = X1 @ np.random.normal(0,1/np.sqrt(2), size=(3,2)) fig4 = go.Figure( go.Scatter3d(x=X1[:,0], y=X1[:,1], z=X1[:,2], mode='markers', showlegend = False, marker=dict(size=5, color=[i for i in range(5)]), name="3D data") ) fig4.add_trace( go.Scatter3d(x=X1_proj[:,0], y=X1_proj[:,1], z=np.zeros(5)-2.5, mode='markers', showlegend = False, marker=dict(size=5, symbol='diamond', color=[i for i in range(5)]), name="2D data") ) fig4.update_layout(height=300, width=500, title="JL Lemma from 3D to 2D") fig4.show() ``` ::: :::{.column width="50%" .fragment} ```{python} #| fig-align: center np.random.seed(12) dist = np.zeros(shape=(5000,4)) X1 = np.random.normal(size=(5,3)) dis0 = pairwise_distances(X1) for i in range(5000): X1_proj = X1 @ np.random.normal(0,1/np.sqrt(2), size=(3,2)) dis = pairwise_distances(X1_proj) dist[i,:] = dis[0,1:]/dis0[0,1:] D = [dist[:,i] for i in range(4)] group_labels = ['dist' + str(i) for i in range(4)] import plotly.figure_factory as ff fig5 = ff.create_distplot(D, group_labels, bin_size=.1) fig5.update_layout(height=300, width=500, title="Distribution of distance ratio") fig5.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: # AutoEncoders {background-color="#15797A"} ## AutoEncoders {auto-animate="true"} ### Introduction :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} [![](./img/Autoencoders1.png)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.05991){target='_blank'} [![](./img/Autoencoders2.png)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.03898){target='_blank'} ::: :::{.column width="50%" .incremental} - [**AutoEncoders:**]{.blue} are a type of DNN used for learning efficient codings of input data. - It's an unsupervised learning method that works by compressing data into a lower-dimensional representation (encoding) and then reconstructing it back to its original form (decoding). :::{.fragment} ![](./img/encoded_6.png){fig-align="center"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## AutoEncoders {auto-animate="true"} ### Main components / Loss :::{style="font-size: 80%"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%" .incremental} ![](./img/encoded_6.png){fig-align="center"} - Data: $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$. - [**Encoder:**]{.blue} $E:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ encodes original data into lower-dimensional representation called **Latent Representation**. - [**Decoder:**]{.blue} $D:\mathbb{R}^{d'}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ reconstructs back the original data from their **Latent Representation**. ::: :::{.column width="50%" .incremental .fragment} ### Loss - Training optimal $\color{blue}{E^*}$ and $\color{blue}{D^*}$ networks can be simply formulated as: $$(\color{blue}{E^*},\color{blue}{D^*})=\arg\min_{E,D} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\text{x}_i,D[E(\text{x}_i)]).$$ - This is equivalent to training two neural networks at once. - **AE** is in fact a generalization of PCA, while PCA finds the optimal linear subs-space (hyperplane) for the projected data, **AE** is able to learn non-linear **manifold embedding** [see [Elad Plaut (2018)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.10253){target="_blank"}]. ::: ::: ::: ## AutoEncoders {auto-animate="true"} ### Other types :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - [**Sparse Autoencoders:**]{.blue} $\color{blue}{E^*}$ and $\color{blue}{D^*}$ networks are trained with penalization. - $L_1$ regularization for regression: $$(\color{blue}{E^*},\color{blue}{D^*})=\arg\min_{E,D} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\text{x}_i,D[E(\text{x}_i)])+\lambda\sum|\color{blue}{W}_{E,D}|.$$ - KL divergence for classification: $$(\color{blue}{E^*},\color{blue}{D^*})=\arg\min_{E,D} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\text{x}_i,D[E(\text{x}_i)])+\lambda\sum_{j}\color{blue}{\text{KL}}(p\|\hat{p}_j).$$ ::: ## AutoEncoders {auto-animate="true"} ### Other types :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - [**Denoising Autoencoders:**]{.blue} $\color{blue}{E^*}$ and $\color{blue}{D^*}$ networks are trained just like before, and the noisy input $\tilde{\text{x}}_i$ is obtained by, for example, $\tilde{\text{x}}_i\sim {\cal N}(\text{x}_i,\sigma^2I_d).$ ![](./img/denosing_ae.png){width=450 fig-align="center"} - [**Variational Autoencoders (VAE)**]{.blue}: see for example, [Diederik P. Kingma and Max Welling (2019)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.02691){target="_blank"}.
